objectives: Trace one autonomic signal across a synapse: release, crossing the gap, docking on a receptor, and how the gap is cleared.

Name each branch's messenger and its receptors: acetylcholine on M receptors; noradrenaline mainly on alpha-1, alpha-2 and beta-1 receptors; and adrenaline, the adrenal glands' hormone, which also reaches beta-2.
Predict how the heart, arterioles, airways and pupil answer each receptor type.
Predict what agonists, antagonists and cholinesterase inhibitors do to heart rate, blood pressure, airways and pupils, including the baroreflex's answer.

mag.prompt: A muscarinic agonist docks on M receptors and switches them on, like extra acetylcholine everywhere at once. What happens to the heart rate and the pupils?
choices: The heart slows and the pupils get smaller
The heart speeds up and the pupils get larger
The heart slows and the pupils get larger
Nothing changes: only nerves can switch receptors on
mag.why: M receptors are the brake's receptors. Switching them all on presses the brake everywhere: the pacemaker slows, and the pupil's ring muscle tightens, so the pupil shrinks. The airways narrow too.

mant.prompt: Atropine sits in M receptors without switching them on, so acetylcholine cannot dock. At rest the heart's brake is always partly on. What happens to the heart rate?
choices: It rises: the brake is released
It falls: the brake is pressed harder
It stays the same: the accelerator is unchanged
mant.why: At rest, acetylcholine on the pacemaker's M receptors holds the rate down. Block those receptors and the brake comes off, so the heart beats faster even though nothing was added to the accelerator.

che.prompt: A cholinesterase inhibitor stops the enzyme that chops acetylcholine apart. The nerves release the same amount as before. What happens at the M receptors?
choices: More acetylcholine docks for longer, so every M effect grows
Less acetylcholine docks, so the brake lets go
The receptors are blocked, as with atropine
Only the heart's receptors change
che.why: With the enzyme stopped, acetylcholine builds up in the gap and keeps docking. The brake is pressed harder everywhere it acts: a slower heart, smaller pupils and narrower airways.

aag.prompt: Phenylephrine switches on alpha-1 receptors on arteriole muscle. It does not act on the heart. What does the heart rate do?
choices: It falls: pressure rises and the baroreflex slows the heart
It rises: alpha-1 receptors speed the heart
It stays the same: the drug does not touch the heart
aag.why: The arterioles narrow and blood pressure rises. The pressure sensors report it, and the brainstem eases the accelerator and presses the brake, so the heart slows: a reflex slowing.

ablock.prompt: An alpha-1 blocker lets arteriole muscle relax, so blood pressure falls. The heart's beta-1 receptors are untouched. What does the heart rate do?
choices: It rises: the baroreflex presses the accelerator
It falls: the blocker reaches the heart
It stays the same
ablock.why: Falling pressure makes the sensors fire less, so the brainstem presses the accelerator. Its noradrenaline still reaches the free beta-1 receptors, and the heart speeds up.

bag.prompt: Isoproterenol switches on both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors. Beta-1 receptors sit on the heart; beta-2 on airway muscle and some arterioles. What happens to the airways?
choices: They widen
They narrow
They do not change: no sympathetic nerves reach them
bag.why: Beta-2 receptors relax airway muscle, which is how adrenaline in the blood widens the airways. A drug that switches them on does the same, even with no nerve nearby, while beta-1 speeds and strengthens the heart.

bblock.prompt: A nonselective beta-blocker covers beta-1 receptors on the heart and beta-2 receptors on airway muscle. What happens to the heart rate and the airways?
choices: The heart slows, and the airways can narrow
The heart slows, and the airways widen
The heart speeds up, and the airways narrow
The heart slows, and the airways are untouched
bblock.why: Without beta-1 signals the heart beats slower and less forcefully. Without beta-2 signals adrenaline can no longer relax airway muscle, so acetylcholine's narrowing wins, which is why these drugs are a danger in asthma.

quiz.stem: Which messenger do parasympathetic nerves release onto organs, and which receptors does it dock on?
choices: Acetylcholine, on muscarinic (M) receptors
Noradrenaline, on beta receptors
Acetylcholine, on alpha receptors
Adrenaline, on muscarinic receptors
quiz.why: The brake's messenger is acetylcholine, and on organs it docks on muscarinic receptors. Noradrenaline, the accelerator's messenger, docks on alpha and beta receptors.

quiz.stem: How does each messenger's signal end?
choices: Acetylcholine is chopped by cholinesterase in the gap; noradrenaline is mostly pumped back into the nerve ending
Both are chopped by cholinesterase in the gap
Both are pumped back into the nerve ending
Neither ends on its own: the receptors switch themselves off
quiz.why: Cholinesterase waits in the gap and chops acetylcholine within moments. No enzyme in the gap chops noradrenaline; the nerve ending pumps most of it back in, which is reuptake.

quiz.stem: Where do alpha-2 receptors sit in this lesson, and what do they do when noradrenaline docks on them?
choices: On the sympathetic nerve ending itself: they turn further release down
On heart muscle: they speed the heart
On airway muscle: they widen the airways
On the pupil's ring muscle: they shrink the pupil
quiz.why: Alpha-2 receptors on the nerve ending are a brake built into the accelerator: noradrenaline docking there reduces how much more is released. Lesson 4's central alpha-2 agonists use the same receptor type in the brainstem.

quiz.stem: Which pairing correctly matches the airway muscle's receptors to their effects?
choices: M receptors narrow the airways; beta-2 receptors widen them
M receptors widen the airways; beta-2 receptors narrow them
Alpha-1 receptors widen the airways; beta-1 receptors narrow them
Beta-1 receptors widen the airways; M receptors have no effect
quiz.why: Acetylcholine from parasympathetic nerves tightens airway muscle through M receptors. Adrenaline in the blood relaxes it through beta-2 receptors. Beta-1 receptors belong to the heart.

quiz.stem: Eye drops that switch on alpha-1 receptors are put in before a doctor looks inside the eye. Why do they help?
choices: They tighten the spoke-like muscle, so the pupil widens
They tighten the ring muscle, so the pupil shrinks
They block the M receptors on the spoke-like muscle
They slow the heart, so less blood clouds the eye
quiz.why: The pupil's spoke-like muscle carries alpha-1 receptors, and switching them on pulls the pupil larger. The ring muscle, with M receptors, is what makes it smaller.

quiz.stem: A patient's heart is beating too slowly because the vagus nerve, a parasympathetic nerve, is firing hard. Which drug speeds it up by acting on the receptors that nerve uses?
choices: Atropine, a muscarinic antagonist
A beta-blocker
A cholinesterase inhibitor
A muscarinic agonist
quiz.why: The vagus slows the heart through acetylcholine on M receptors. Atropine blocks those receptors and releases the brake. A cholinesterase inhibitor or a muscarinic agonist would slow the heart further, and so would a beta-blocker.

quiz.stem: Someone starts an alpha-1 blocker for high blood pressure. Which change in heart rate is expected, and why?
choices: Faster: falling pressure makes the baroreflex press the accelerator
Slower: the blocker covers the heart's beta-1 receptors
Slower: alpha-1 receptors are the heart's accelerator
No change: nothing reaches the heart
quiz.why: The blocker widens arterioles, so pressure falls. The baroreflex answers by pressing the accelerator, and its noradrenaline reaches the free beta-1 receptors on the heart. The speed-up is the reflex, not the drug acting on the heart.

quiz.stem: A person with asthma is prescribed a nonselective beta-blocker. Why is this risky?
choices: It blocks beta-2 receptors, so adrenaline can no longer relax airway muscle
It switches on M receptors in the airways
It stops cholinesterase, so acetylcholine builds up in the airways
It speeds the heart, which tires the breathing muscles
quiz.why: Airway muscle relies on beta-2 receptors, fed by adrenaline in the blood, to relax. A nonselective beta-blocker covers them too, so the airways can narrow. Beta-1-selective drugs spare the airways more.

takeaways: The autonomic nervous system runs the organs without thought, through two branches: the sympathetic accelerator and the parasympathetic brake. Most organs get both; most blood vessels get only the accelerator.
At a synapse a nerve ending releases a messenger that crosses a tiny gap and docks on receptors; the signal fades soon after the gap is cleared.
Parasympathetic nerves release acetylcholine onto muscarinic (M) receptors, and cholinesterase in the gap chops it apart within moments.

Most sympathetic nerves release noradrenaline onto alpha and beta receptors (those to sweat glands release acetylcholine). Its signal ends mostly by reuptake into the nerve ending, and alpha-2 receptors on the ending turn release down. The adrenal glands add adrenaline to the blood.
M: slower heart, narrower airways, smaller pupil. Beta-1: faster, stronger heart. Alpha-1: narrower arterioles, larger pupil. Beta-2: wider airways and some wider arterioles.

Agonists switch receptors on and antagonists block them. Cholinesterase inhibitors make acetylcholine linger, which strengthens its signal wherever it is released: at M receptors, and at skeletal muscle, where too much causes weakness.
The baroreflex answers a drug's effect on blood pressure: alpha-1 agonists raise pressure and slow the heart; alpha-1 blockers lower it and speed the heart.
Nonselective beta-blockers slow and weaken the heart and can narrow the airways in asthma by blocking beta-2 receptors; beta-1-selective ones spare the airways more.
